idiom_name: mapper layer: per-aggregate mappers + mapping descriptor + session (identity map / unit of work)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give each aggregate a mapper that owns the object-relational translation and the load/save operations, and keep the mapping declaration (annotations, external descriptor or an imperative mapping call) outside the domain types. Hand the mapper a session that supplies the identity map and the unit of work, so one row becomes exactly one object per transaction and writes are flushed in dependency order. All SQL, table and column names and conversion of value objects stay behind the mapper interface; the domain module must not import the mapper. Where the stack already ships such a session (JPA/Hibernate, EF Core, SQLAlchemy, MikroORM), use it rather than rebuilding identity and change tracking by hand.
code_sketch:
class CustomerMapper:                       # the layer: one mapper per aggregate
    load(id)            -> Customer          # rows -> object (columns, value objects, links)
    insert/update/delete(Customer)           # object -> rows

session:  identity_map {row_key -> object}   # one object per row
transaction: [new | dirty | removed]         # unit of work, flushed in dependency order

# application code:
customer = session.customers.get(id)         # mapper + identity map
customer.rename("Ada")                        # domain behaviour, no persistence knowledge
session.commit()                             # writes go through the mappers
pitfalls: Letting the domain call the mapper, or hand a session/connection to a domain object, destroys persistence ignorance faster than any other shortcut.
A mapper used without an identity map rebuilds objects per query, so two queries for the same row produce two objects and relationship graphs become inconsistent.

Mapping metadata inside the domain type (annotations, mandatory base classes) re-couples the model to the schema and to the mapper's constraints - no-arg constructors, proxyable classes, settable fields.

Cyclic references between aggregates (A has B, B has A) cause infinite recursive loads if the identity map is not populated with a ghost before recursion; Fowler calls this out on page 169-170 of PEAA - register an empty shell in the identity map before loading its children.

Proxy identity trap: two lazy proxies for the same database row compare as not-equal (reference equality) even though they represent the same entity; override equals() by primary key and ensure the session's identity map returns the same proxy instance.

N+1 ripple loading: loading a collection then iterating it with a per-item lazy-load trigger fires 1+N SQL queries; Fowler calls this ripple loading - the most common ORM performance killer. Fix with batch or join fetch, not per-item lazy loads.

Implicit cartesian explosion: loading multiple collections with a join fetch (A hasMany B, A hasMany C) produces a cartesian product; ORM may load one collection correctly while silently dropping rows from the other. Fix with split queries (EF Core AsSplitQuery, Hibernate's Set vs List semantics, or @BatchSize for batched sub-queries).

Metadata drift: mapping annotations or fluent config that silently diverge from the actual schema (renamed column, dropped index, changed type) produces nulls or truncated values with no exception; detect with schema validation at startup or contract tests against the real database.

Transaction scope mismatch: opening a session per business transaction is correct for a Unit of Work, but sharing a session across multiple business transactions (or using a new session per query) causes stale data, phantom reads and incorrect identity map behaviour.
Dirty reading across bounded contexts: a mapper that loads a cross-context entity and mutates it without event-sourced reconciliation can corrupt another context's view of the same database row.

Batch flush ordering: when a Unit of Work processes new, dirty and removed objects in the wrong dependency order (child before parent insert, parent before child delete) the database raises foreign-key violations; maintain a topological sort of aggregate dependency at flush time.

Soft-delete / logical delete confusion: mapper queries that return 'active' rows only, but ORM-level identity map or second-level cache still holds the logically-deleted instance; queries return the cached copy instead of the database result, bypassing the where clause.

Hibernate MultipleBagFetchException: fetching two or more @OneToMany List collections simultaneously via JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph throws at startup; Hibernate treats unordered Lists as bags and a cartesian product would result. Fix: change List to Set, or split into two queries in the same transaction (Hibernate merges results via first-level cache).

EF Core shadow-state pollution: implicit shadow properties (FKs, audit fields) tracked only in the change tracker are invisible to domain logic that operates on detached entities; serialising and re-attaching an entity loses shadow values unless explicitly re-populated.

SQLAlchemy AsyncSession outside transaction scope: awaiting a lazy-load attribute on an async session after the session has closed raises LazyLoadingError; always materialise collections inside the explicit async with block or use raise_on_none for async access.

EF Core navigation fixup side-effects: when attaching a graph where some entities already exist in the identity map, EF Core silently performs relationship fixup - setting navigation properties to tracked instances even when the incoming graph had different references; this can cause identity split if the code later relies on object reference equality.

Hibernate bytecode-enhancement vs proxy clash: entities enhanced for lazy attribute loading (FieldHandled style) conflict with proxy-based lazy loading on the same association; pick one strategy per mapping, not both, to avoid ClassCastException at access time.

Async session scope mismatch: awaiting a lazy-load attribute on an AsyncSession after the session has closed raises LazyLoadingError; always materialise collections inside the explicit async with block and use session.execute() with select() rather than the legacy query API.

expire_on_commit=True (SQLAlchemy default): after a commit, all objects are marked expired and accessing any attribute triggers an implicit synchronous SQL query — forbidden in async code; always set expire_on_commit=False in async sessions.

Async implicit async-to-sync bridge: using synchronous SQLAlchemy ORM operations inside an async function (e.g. relationship attributes accessed without await) silently bridges to sync execution, blocking the event loop; catch with PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1.

Hibernate bytecode-enhancement vs proxy clash: entities enhanced for lazy attribute loading (FieldHandled style) conflict with proxy-based lazy loading on the same association; pick one strategy per mapping, not both, to avoid ClassCastException at access time.

Soft-delete / logical delete confusion: mapper queries that return 'active' rows only, but ORM-level identity map or second-level cache still holds the logically-deleted instance; queries return the cached copy instead of the database result, bypassing the where clause.

Batch flush ordering: when a Unit of Work processes new, dirty and removed objects in the wrong dependency order (child before parent insert, parent before child delete) the database raises foreign-key violations; maintain a topological sort of aggregate dependency at flush time.
Dirty reading across bounded contexts: a mapper that loads a cross-context entity and mutates it without event-sourced reconciliation can corrupt another context's view of the same database row.

MapStruct vs ModelMapper performance: ModelMapper uses runtime reflection and is ~300x slower than MapStruct for large list mappings; prefer MapStruct for any production mapping layer with non-trivial data volumes.

Implicit cartesian explosion: loading multiple @OneToMany List collections with JOIN FETCH produces a cartesian product that silently drops rows from one collection; Hibernate MultipleBagFetchException is the runtime symptom; fix with Set, split queries, or @OrderColumn.

EF Core AsNoTracking identity resolution: using AsNoTracking() on queries that return entities already in the change tracker produces a new detached instance, breaking equality checks; use AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution() when you need tracking for already-loaded entities.

SQLAlchemy 2.0 unique() requirement: ORM results from queries must be deduplicated by calling .unique() on SelectResult when the query can produce duplicate rows (e.g. joined eager loading of one-to-many relationships); failure to call .unique() raises orm_exc.DetachedInstanceError on related access.

aiosqlite write amplification: SQLite via aiosqlite has reduced write throughput compared to asyncpg/aiomysql; for write-heavy async workloads prefer PostgreSQL with asyncpg or MySQL with aiomysql over SQLite.

AsyncSession per-request anti-pattern: creating a new AsyncSession for each query (instead of per-transaction) defeats the identity map and causes duplicate objects for the same row within a single request; scope sessions per business transaction, not per query.

Hibernate @BatchSize global vs per-entity: setting hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size globally applies batch loading to all entities uniformly, which may over-fetch for small look-up tables; prefer @BatchSize(size=N) annotations on specific associations for targeted control.

EF Core shadow-state pollution: implicit shadow properties (FKs, audit fields) tracked only in the change tracker are invisible to domain logic on detached entities; serialising and re-attaching an entity loses shadow values unless explicitly re-populated.

N+1 ripple loading: loading a collection then iterating it with a per-item lazy-load trigger fires 1+N SQL queries; Fowler calls this ripple loading - the most common ORM performance killer. Fix with batch or join fetch, not per-item lazy loads.

Wrong move: adding ORM lifecycle callbacks, finder methods or a session reference to domain objects 'just for one query' -> persistence ignorance silently erodes and the model becomes Active Record with mapper overhead on top -> instead keep every query, callback and flush in the mapper/infrastructure layer and construct or reconstitute domain objects through mappers or factories.

Wrong move: treating persist()/remove() (Doctrine EntityManager) or equivalent registration calls as the write -> SQL is only executed at flush(), so forgetting flush() loses changes and a flush in the middle of a loop writes a partial unit of work -> instead commit once per business transaction and treat flush as the explicit Unit of Work boundary (0-2 flushes per request is the Doctrine guidance).

Wrong move: leaving every managed entity on full implicit change tracking -> on every flush the UnitOfWork diffs a copy of every managed object's state, so read-heavy requests pay linear memory and CPU for rows they never update -> instead mark insert-only or never-updated entities read-only or use explicit change-tracking policies (e.g. Doctrine READ_ONLY / CHANGE_TRACKING_DEFERRED_EXPLICIT) so flush skips them.
